title: Finding A Balance
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating equanimity and radical acceptance in order to live a life of compassion and virtue. By letting go of preconceptions and attachments, we can respond skillfully and authentically to the present moment, creating opportunities for growth and connection with others. This requires embracing our natural tendencies and allowing ourselves to be guided by our hearts, rather than being controlled by self-centered desires or outcomes.
topics: Native American story (e.g. Sue Ann Big Crow)

sentences.text: Good evening everyone.
I'm Eko Jeff Kelley from the Seattle area, from the Seattle Soto Zen community down there.
Tim and I have been talking about an exchange like this for quite some time, so it's really nice to finally get up here.
He's been down there once in the last year at least.
And of course you know that we're doing a sesshin together, rohatsu sesshin, coming up in the first week in December.
I hope many of you can fit that into your schedule.
Tonight I'd like to talk about two of the principal teachings in Zen, probably in Buddhism, and how to integrate them.
Probably these are the two teachings of Zen, if I could go out on a limb and say that.
Basically they are radically accepting everything that is happening in our life, and stepping forward and acting for the benefit of all beings.
These two things can seem contradictory.
One is just radical acceptance of the way things are, and the other is working, in a compassionate and skillful way, for the benefit of all beings.
I know in my practice early on I asked that question, and I probably still ask it, and I get asked it quite often.
So I'd like to explore how to put these two together tonight.
That first teaching of radical acceptance can be stated another way, one that's quite well known in our tradition, by [unclear: "Jinjure Singsung San"], the third patriarch.
He's the third generation after Bodhidharma, and he wrote a sutra or a poem called Trust in Mind, [unclear: "Jinjin Ming"].
It begins with this:
*The ultimate path is without difficulty, just avoid picking and choosing, just don't love or hate and you'll be lucid and clear.*
Or a more recent translation:
*The great way is not difficult for those who have no preferences.
When love and hate are both absent, everything becomes clear and undisguised.*
So this "have no preferences" thing, "avoid picking and choosing," is a statement of just opening up to the way things are, allowing things to rise and pass away without meddling with them.
And this is the teaching of equanimity.
Things pass through our lives, and to a certain extent, in a certain way, we are made upright as these things come and go, these external events and these internal mental phenomena.
My teacher back in Minnesota likes to talk about the eight worldly winds.
I don't know if you're familiar with that teaching, but there are four dichotomies: pleasure and pain, gain and loss, fame and ill repute, success and failure.
These things are always blowing through our lives, and we're usually chasing after one or resisting another.
At least that's the way our conditioning compels us to move.
What my teacher likes to say is that these winds are the melody of our life.
It's not the whole, it's not all the music, but it's the melody, and it rises and falls.
Sometimes it's loud, sometimes it's very soft and delicate.

As for this picking and choosing, one reason I think we are admonished against it is that, if you stop and think about it, as I see it, as soon as we exert a preference, we constellate this separated self, this self that is separated from the rest of the universe.
It's as if we carry this conditioning with us, a predisposition toward reacting a certain way.
Then some external trigger comes along, and all of a sudden our preference is engaged.
And I think in a certain way it's not until then that this separated self is constellated.
The minute we have a preference, and it's me who wants something, then we're already in the realm of suffering.
We're wanting something that we don't have.
I think we know this.
This is one of the basic teachings, right?
I have a little story that relates to this.
About a year ago, I was invited to John Bastyr College, or university, a local university in the Seattle area.
One of the teachers invited me to come in and speak about Zen and Buddhist meditation.
That's not too uncommon.
So I went there, brought my zabuton and my zafu, and set them up on a table in front of the class.
We did our meditation instruction and we all meditated.
This was a world religion class.
We had some discussion, and then about halfway through, I was asking for questions, and the teacher said, "Well, I have a question.
There's this story that I've been thinking about and working on, and I'm wondering what your reaction to it would be."
So he tells the story.
In a distant time in a distant land, there is a famous archer, very skilled in archery and renowned throughout the land as the greatest archer around.
He's riding through the countryside one day and he sees a big barn with all these targets painted on it.
In each target, in the very center of the bullseye, there's one arrow.
The more he looks, the more he sees all these targets with an arrow right in the center of the bullseye.
This gets him thinking: who is this archer that is using these for practice?
So he rides over to the farm and finds the owner of the farm and says, "I'm noted for my skill in archery, but I'm really impressed by whoever is shooting these arrows around here.
I really want to meet them."
The farmer says, "No, no, no, trust me, you don't want to meet this guy."
"No, I'm serious.
I really want to meet him."
Again the archer insists.
And so the [unclear: "pharmacist"] says, "Okay, let me tell you about it.
His name is Schmiel," I think that was the name this guy used.
"He's not what you think.
What he does is shoot the arrow first and then paint the bullseye around it."
So he's more of a painter, actually, than an archer.
The teacher wondered what I thought of this, and we chewed on it for a while.
I thought, well, in a way this is like our teaching of just radically accepting everything.
Wherever the arrow is, we receive it as a bullseye.
All these disjointed and painful and pleasant things in our life, each one can be a bullseye if we receive it that way.
Each one is right here, right where it's supposed to be.
So this is, I think, sort of a teaching of equanimity.
We played with that for a while and had a good class.
At the end we'd said our thank yous and goodbyes, and I was carrying my zafu, zabuton out the door.
There were several seats right by the door, the little school-desk type things.
As I was walking out, my zabuton knocked over someone's cup of tea right by the door.
I was halfway past before I realized it, and I turned to say something about, life is always like this, isn't it?
Something.
And instead one of the students said, "Bullseye."
So I just bowed and left.
Not only was it very apt, but it was actually also very compassionate for me, who had made this blunder and was worried about it, and for the student whose tea had spilled.
So we can do this, right?
We can create bullseyes wherever life takes us.
Anyway, that's just one expression of this teaching of equanimity, of radical acceptance.
The other teaching that we're working on tonight, doing for the benefit of all beings, can be summarized in another famous little story.
A monk asked Yun Men, "What are the teachings of a lifetime?"
And Yun Men answered, "An appropriate statement," or also, "An appropriate response."
So what is it all about?
It's about an appropriate response: responding in the way that the circumstances call us to respond.
This is, at least, a different energy than just saying, "Whatever happens, I'm right here for it."
This is stepping forward, doing something.
So in one case we have, it's all about just receiving this and not picking and choosing.
In the second case we have, it's all about responding in a skillful, compassionate way.
I think these are expressions of two main teachings, a sort of wisdom and compassion thing.
How do we put them together in our life?
How do we put them together in our mental experience?
When we sit down on the cushion, what is right effort and right action, and how does this all work?
That's what we're going to look at tonight.
One author that I appreciate is Peter Hershock.
I don't know if you know him, but he writes on Chan Buddhism, which is Chinese Zen.
Zen really becomes Zen in China, and that's where the great flowering of Zen happens, or at least one of the first great flowerings.
Most of our koans come from that time period, and then later it goes to Japan.
Peter Hershock writes about the essence of Chinese Zen, which would be the essence of Zen in general.
He talks about virtuosity.
Realization is not something that's achieved or acquired.
It's something that's done.
So it's the constant doing, this constant virtuosity and harmonizing with the circumstances we find ourselves in.
That's an expression of that second teaching.
So how to put them together?
We know certain ways that don't work very well.
My first teacher talked about how in the early days of the Zen center they would want to order a pizza, and they'd be standing around and they'd say, "Well, what kind of pizza should we order?"
And everybody would say, "It doesn't matter to me.
It doesn't matter to me."
No one could bring themselves to express a preference, so ordering a pizza was really difficult.
This is not what we're talking about.
This is not putting them together in a skillful way.
So how do we do it?
Certainly there is some sort of discernment when we step forward into the world and act skillfully, or attempt to.
We have to discern a path, and in a way that's a choice between various things that we could do.
So there's a certain following of one way over another, but I think it has quite a different energy.
So here's another story.
This one I read in a book, but it comes from the Pine Ridge Indian reservation in South Dakota.
It's the site of Wounded Knee, which was the site of an Indian massacre in the late 19th century, and also the site of an occupation by the American Indian Movement in the mid seventies.
So it has quite a history in the conflict between the Europeans and the Native Americans.
This story has to do with the Pine Ridge girls basketball team in the mid 1980s, and it involves one particular young woman named Sue Ann Big Crow.
I think this is an example of what we're talking about: how to put these two together and act in the world.
The Pine Ridge girls team was going to play at a nearby school in Lead, South Dakota, which is in the Black Hills.
Lead is a mining town, and it grew up around the gold mine.
Gold was discovered in the Black Hills in like 1860 or something like that, and the minute it was discovered, the U.S.
Cavalry was sent in, led by George Custer, and the Indians were essentially pushed out of this sacred land.

So the site of this basketball game is centered around the gold mine, the discovery of which was really the reason that the Indians were pushed out of this very fertile and productive Black Hills and onto this more barren landscape where the Pine Ridge Indian reservation is now.
It's a very bleak place.
So they're going to play in the other school's gymnasium, and there's quite a bit of rivalry.
Actually, there's a lot of ill feeling and racial tension between the two.
They're going into Lead, South Dakota, and before they're set to go out onto the court, the stands are packed and there's all this hooting and hollering.
These hometown fans are mocking the Indian women, making all these silly and cruel and stupid, anyway, derogatory sounds and statements, yelling out about squaws and stuff.
The stands are pounding and there's all this racket going on.
The girls basketball team is standing inside, and the person who usually goes out first, who is the tallest person, a senior, just says, "I don't think I can handle this.
I just don't want to go out there."
Yeah.
So this young woman, Suann Big Crow, who was only a freshman or something, and one of the shorter members of the team, says, "Okay, let me do it."
And the senior says, "No, I don't know.
Are you sure you want to do this?"
She says, "Yes, I want to do this."
Usually what they do is run onto the court and take a lap and then do some layups and then go back to their bench.
So Suann takes the ball, and they're dressed in their warmups, and she leads the team out to mid court and then stops, and everybody kind of bumps up.
They're not anticipating a stop there.
Meanwhile, the stands are yelling insults and such.

So Suann tosses the ball to a teammate, and right there in the center of the basketball court, in the circle, where the jump ball happens, she takes off her warmup jacket and starts doing this shawl dance.
The shawl dance is a traditional Indian dance that young women do with a ceremonial shawl that they twist and work with in the dance.
So she starts doing this dance with her warmup jacket as a shawl.
And she starts singing in Lakota, and all of a sudden the stands, the room, is dead quiet.
She's doing this beautiful dance with the shawl, and people are sort of dumbstruck.
They're just transported.
So she does this for a while.
And then finally she puts the jacket over her shoulders and leads the team down around the court, and the gymnasium breaks out in applause.
The relationship between these teams is really dramatically transformed for years to come, even amongst the parents.
For me, this is a virtuosic performance, and it's so great because it unifies, right?
It plays to the common humanity and the common dignity and the common response to beauty that all these people share.
It's not about selfishness.
It's not about asserting one thing over another.
It's just doing this beautiful thing.
And it's just taking the very ingredients of the moment, right?
The warmup jacket and the basketball court.
With just this little thing, transforming people's lives and certainly transforming the game and the days to come.
So let's use that as an example and take a closer look at it.

I think, standing in that locker room or whatever before that, with the noise outside, we would tend to be frightened into our fixed views, and we would tend not to want to trust the universe at this point, and all those rigid positions that we retreat to when we're afraid.
This was a totally different response.
Peter Herschach again talks about simultaneously listening and responding.
As in a jazz improvisation, it's like receiving radically without trying to change anything and using those ingredients for the dance and for the improv.
So: listening and doing simultaneously, receiving and doing simultaneously, and having to, well, each moment, right?
Just flow with those things, combining virtuosity and intimacy.
Another image that I like is the patterning in a stone or a piece of wood.
It's a record of its conditions arising, and it's also an illustration of the natural dispositions by which it can be shaped into something beautiful.

So it's as if each moment has a grain to it that we can either work against and muddle through and come out with something that doesn't fit at all with the grain, or we can flow with the grain of the moment and of the circumstances and let the grain dictate the sculpture.
I think the integration of these two things really comes down to our Buddha nature, our luminous, compassionate heart, our unobstructed nature.
I like the word unobstructed because an obstruction is a barrier to action.
So this luminous nature that we have is not a static thing.
It's not a thing we just sort of dissolve into.
There's an active component to it.
I hadn't thought about it that way until recently: our open, deepest luminous heart, it's not just a thing.
It has a doing as well.
And maybe after all it just comes down to the word love.
Maybe we can view that word a little differently if it's become kind of worn out, but isn't love receiving and doing and not getting stuck in one or the other?
And yet we're human beings, right?
We have our foibles and our fears and our preferences.
Rather than ridding ourselves of all these things before we can engage in this action, I think if we simply include them as the ingredients of our life, we can do that dance, tell another story.
But I think I will end.
In ending, I really appreciate the way Bernie Glassman phrases the three treasures, Buddha, Dharma, Sangha.
The way he puts it, for Buddha, it's not knowing.
For Dharma, it is bearing witness.
And for Sangha, it's loving action.
For me, it's almost a sequential thing.
The not knowing is the dropping of all preconceptions and the dropping of the resistance to the way things are.
The bearing witness is the actual listening and opening and receiving, deeply, the sound of the beings around us, the voice of all the beings that surround us.
And the loving action is then as if it flows forth.
It naturally follows the grain, if we see the obstructions clearly enough and
**Eko Jeff Kelley:** As we see them, they sort of fall away.
So we don't really have to worry about it, right?
We have this idea of stepping off the hundred-foot pole.
And now there's more to the story.
We can't just stand on top of the hundred-foot pole.
We have to step off it.
So what does stepping off require?
Well, it requires a tremendous trust in the way things are, right?
A trust that the universe will come forth and support us.
So there's the step, which is the action.
And then there's the trust, which is really what equanimity is also about.
It's just receiving it without needing to push away or grasp or change it to suit our own personal perceived needs.
And of course this is the practice of a lifetime.
This integration, this shedding of the armor around our heart, the trust that allows us to just flow forth in a wise and compassionate way.
I would be interested in comments or questions or any kind of discussion.
You can do a little improvising together, maybe.
Yes.
**Participant:** How do we get the bullseye possible every instant with the, what you were playing to with that?
We're human and we have selfless understanding and we have habits and reaction.
So if we're engaged in that, how is that bullseye?
How do we get?
**Eko Jeff Kelley:** Well, that's a good question.
I think we learn gradually to let go and to trust and then to act.
And at first, maybe it's just a glimmer and we'll tighten back up.
But then maybe we will, just for a few seconds, be spontaneous, which I think we can point to in our life, in our past times when we've just responded very skillfully and spontaneously.
And then inevitably our habit patterns and our self-centeredness comes in and clenches back up.
But I think, and this is where Zazen helps, right?
Zazen is continually letting this moment be a bullseye and letting go of preferences.
So I think it's like a muscle we exercise.
And we get better at just letting go and acting.
And then we know also that when we clench back up or tighten back up, that's really not separate.
It's really all part of the whole.

If we divide it in half, saying, well, this is what I was just doing, this wonderful, virtuosic behavior, and this is bad old human self-centeredness, as soon as we do that, then we're at war with ourselves again.
And so it's that backward step continually: oh yeah, these are ingredients too.
Oh yeah, you have your preconceptions and I have mine.
How can we make those part of the dance?
So I don't know if that helps at all.
Anybody else?
**Participant:** And yet there's action.
Things are happening.
There's doing going on, right?
And then, but how do you, so we find ourselves there once in a while, develop that kind of moment.
It feels right.
Right.
Right.
Right.
Right.
Right.
**Eko Jeff Kelley:** Well, you're already noticing that.
So that's good.
I think it's natural.
I think that's our conditioning: to not let go.
Right.
And as soon as we do anything that resembles that, and just have this little dance for a moment, then that sets off all these alarms.
Right.
And we come back later on and go, oh God, how could I say that?
Oh, that's so stupid.
But just to know that.
Yeah.
I used to give talks, and the talk went fine, but then afterwards it's like, oh God, the last thing I wanted to do was listen to one of my talks.
So I know exactly what you're saying.
But I think, again, those patterns, right?
We see the patterns and we get to know the patterns.
And when we see them doing their thing, we can interrupt them.
And we can settle back into this state of equanimity, or at least touch it a little again.
Those patterns start to lose their energy.
Right.
And then these other, more wholesome patterns start to gain in energy.
So I think it's a long, long process, because these patterns are so deep, right?
I mean, they happen long before we're aware of it.
But I think through Zazen we learn at least to see it, and that step forward might just be interrupting, saying, do something different.
What about one back?
**Participant:** Just get out and vote.
**Eko Jeff Kelley:** Yeah.
Well, I think you close your eyes, right?
No.
Yeah.
No, you're right.
We have to make choices, right?
In order to participate in this world, where we engage in it as a separate human being, we need to make choices.
So one thing we can do is just do the best we can and say, well, I can't see how Buddha, I don't know how Buddha would have voted.
I'm going to look as deeply into my heart as I can.
I'm going to call up whatever I have learned about my preconceptions about the way the world should be and about the way other people should be.
And I'm going to get to know my anger about, you know, these people are so stupid.

So if we can get to know that reactivity that pushes us all around and be more comfortable in that state of equanimity, then I think even though we're picking and choosing, we're much closer to a grounded, compassionate choice.
So we can begin to feel what the grain of the situation might be.
Because we're [unclear: "so politics"], especially, right?
We're so reactive and it gets our blood going, right?
How could they say such a thing?
I think that reactivity is not so helpful.
So if we learn how it pushes us down roads that are not so helpful, at least it's a step in that direction.

Well, no, I think I know, I think, well, I'd say that again, there's a different energy between that self-centered preference, which I think, every time that happens, splits the universe into me and the rest of the world, right?
Because I want something or I don't want something.
So there's me and the thing out there, and that reinforces the separation that we feel.
And there's that movement of the heart, which is not just a blah, splat.
It has a direction to it.
It wants to harmonize, right?
There is a way that we can learn to follow that, I think, which does not reinforce that separateness, that barrier.
It actually helps dissolve the barrier.
So to me, there's a different quality of energy there, and it doesn't really matter what words we use, right?
Because you can say, well, yeah, that's a preference, but how does it feel?
And what are the results of that?
I think that's a better basis on which to go one way or another.
So that's preference in the heart, right?
Is that kind of what you mean?
Nancy.
Yeah.
It's just making me think about attachment to outcome.
We do have to make choices, but I think the suffering comes when we're attached to the outcome of the choice.
We're insistent that, okay, if I'm going to vote this way, this guy better win, or this gal.
And when they don't, I'm curious.
That's the suffering.
It's not so much, okay, I'm going to choose the best that I believe would be good for the world, whatever, but I can't attach to the outcome unless I really want to suffer.
Right.
So that's quite far from equanimity, right?
When we're attached to the outcome.
Because we learn that we get smacked around pretty good, particularly on election night.
I was thinking that perhaps hunting might be an example of what you were pondering.

I wonder if this hunting, so when you say the preference of the heart that divides you off, then that would be your own personal preference that was rooted in your desire for your own security or pleasure.

And then I just wonder, maybe hunting, having a preference that there be no hunters in the world, could be, maybe that could be a preference at the heart, because it's not really about your own self-preservation and separating you off.
Well, I think we each have to investigate that, right?
And I can see how it could be, but it's hard to say.
So to investigate the [unclear: "cell"], the degree of self that is invested in that desire.
I mean, how do you feel towards hunters, for instance?
If you can love the hunters, then you're on your way.

I just want to share what's helped me, and it's probably taken me a long time to finally become aware of this, but it's getting in touch with my body when I'm about to either respond to react, and I can feel it in my body when it's just a reaction and it's a strong preference.

And realizing that before I speak or before I act, it doesn't always happen, but generally, if I reflect back on it, I can feel either the heat rising or the body constrict, and then I know that I've just reacted to the situation, that it hasn't really come from the heart or hasn't worked itself through that way.
And I think sitting practice really has helped me be more and more aware of that and able to catch it ahead of time.
I don't know.
I think dropping into the awareness of the body, for me the body knows about no separation.
It's like the body is already there in a way.
And when we drop into the body, it gives us a whole new perspective.
I was just thinking about the choice idea, where you choose something and the more things you have.
It's all those toppings for the pizza, right?
No, I'm sorry.
No, if the menu is really long.
Yeah, right.
I hate those.
It just seemed, I guess.
So the [unclear: "competitors have"] in our own mind, is that what you're saying?
Yeah.
Whether it's, yeah, I can see that.
And it's almost a different mode, right?
If we're in the mode of saying, well, do I want this one, this one, this one, this one, no matter what, if we stay in that mode, we're kind of in the realm of suffering, right?
But if the mode is receiving what comes, or allowing somehow that movement of the heart to lead us, then in a sense we are allowing all those choices to drop away.
And even setting the menu aside, right?
Going back into the kitchen and fixing something.
Good.
That is one of the balancing acts.
I agree.
Because I think we are individuals.
We do live this life as individuals and we need to learn how to operate in that realm, compassionately.
But I think our choices as individuals can have one flavor or another.
Our choice as an individual can be from a very self-centered point of view, or it can be from a much more open, grounded, empathic point of view.
Right?
So there are different.
Would you say that makes sense to you?
But I think, yeah.
And in our practice, I think we learn to sort of touch this place where we can experience that interconnection.
And for me, it affects how that linear discriminating mind operates.
It's like we still have to make the choice, but I don't have to be afraid about making the wrong choice.
I don't have to be afraid about what might happen.
I don't have all this reactivity, this stuff that pushes me around when I'm in the act of making that choice.
I think so.

I think there can be a clarity and a just all these non-essential things that don't really relate to that choice: all of our own emotional stuff, or things that come from our past that really don't apply to the situation at hand.
I think if we can let those go and just say, "Yeah, this is this and this is this," it makes a difference.
So thanks.
Because your preferences are part of what is, right?
Is that kind of what you're saying?
Yeah.
And I think in doing that, we're not so pushed around by our preferences, right?
We still can, but we have a little more choice as to whether I want to go this way or not.
There's this story, which I really like, another little Zen story.
You may well know it.
There's one Zen teacher who takes a walk out into the springtime, out into the mountains and fields.
When he comes back, the head monk says, "Where have you been wandering?"
He says, "Oh, I'm strolling about in the hills."
And the head monk says, "Well, where did you go?"
And he says, "Well, first I went following the scented grasses, and then I came back following the falling flowers."
And the head monk said, "Well, that's spring.
That's the spring mood right there."
And the teacher says, "Yes, it's better.
I like it better than the autumn dew falling on the lotus flowers."
And the head monk says, "I'm really grateful for that answer."
So despite all the training in equanimity and the strolling about, receiving whatever comes, he comes back and says, "Yeah, I like spring.
It's great, and actually I like it better than the autumn."
And the monk is really grateful because, wow, we can still be human beings.
Somehow we have to, as you were saying, include those preferences in the way we meet our lives.
We can prefer one kind of pizza to another, right?
I don't want that pizza.
I want something else.
Anybody else?
I've been teaching this class about mindfulness, and I asked to be looking at this question of pleasant.

This fellow said that one of the few pleasures in life for him, and these are people with a lot of physical difficulties, is going to the gym and then going to the wet sauna, the steamer, but he doesn't like the dry sauna.
And so he's about ready to give up and go home.
But he decided, "Well, I'll try the dry sauna."
So I think what we think is not what we want.
And sometimes our preferences are no more than habits, right?
They're not really this sort of alive being that's making choices based on present circumstances.
They would have to compete with each other to give him whatever he wanted so that he liked them better.
It's very, very sad.
Anyway, when that little boy was with me once alone, he said, "I wanted these."
I think at the time it was Pokemon cards or something like that.
He said, "I wanted them so badly.
I just bugged my parents until they got them all for me, and I got them."
And it was so beautiful to see that this little guy realized at such a young age that this isn't what you think.
He gets what he wants, and something with all this stuff.
It still moves my heart today to think of someone so young being so wise.
It's just beautiful.
Maybe the habits won't be so deep in him that he'll be able to shift off that more easily, since he's discovered it at a young age.
**Participant:** Moral self, but I think in terms of my moral self, my personality, my history, it's my physical body.
Then there's this eternal self, which seems universal.
And are you saying that it's important?
I think, well, are you saying that obviously you can't, you don't want to cut any part of this?
**Eko Jeff Kelley:** Yeah.
Well, I'm not sure I do either, but we're not saying one is wrong, right?
If we say that acting according to our preferences is always wrong, then I don't think we want to say that.
And although the lines of the poem that I read pretty much sound that way, the larger poem is about this idea of nonduality.
